title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic Pretraining for VLAs
one_liner: Teach robots to move by learning from throwaway data, then teach them what to do with scarce expert examples.
lead: Vision-Language-Action models (systems that read images, understand text instructions, and pick actions) usually need expensive collections of labeled robot videos showing what to do. This paper separates two things: learning how a robot's body moves in the world, and learning which task to do. By first training on cheap unlabeled robot play—footage that has no task label at all—the model learns the physics of grasping and movement. Then a quick second stage connects those physics to language instructions.

problem.h2: The bottleneck: expensive labeled robot videos
paras: Vision-Language-Action models read images, parse text instructions, and output motor commands to control a robot. Training requires millions of video clips showing a human expert doing a task—moving a gripper, pushing objects, stacking blocks—labeled with the instruction and the exact action at each frame. Collecting these triplets is slow and costly.

A beginner might think the solution is obvious: gather more labeled data. But that just makes the problem worse. The model ends up needing massive labeled datasets to learn even simple moves, because it has to learn physics (how a gripper closes, how objects slide) and task-knowledge (what 'push the block left' means) from scratch, all tangled together. This means building a robot that understands language requires an impossible amount of labeled video.

callout.html: Separate two learning problems: (1) learn how to move from cheap unlabeled robot play, then (2) connect movement to language using minimal expert video.

steps.text: Feed pairs of consecutive frames from unlabeled robot play; train to predict the action between them.
Model discovers what pixels control grasping, how hard contact is, when objects slip, end-effector pose.
Freeze Stage 1 weights; add a decoder and train on small set of expert video + text instruction pairs.
Decoder learns to match language intent to the physical primitives the encoder already knows.
Read image and instruction. Encoder extracts affordances. Decoder picks action that matches intent.

paras: The paper changes the training pipeline: instead of training end-to-end from scratch on labeled data, it breaks training into two stages. Stage 1 trains only the visual encoder using unlabeled robot play. Stage 2 trains the action decoder using minimal expert video. This decoupling means the hard (learning physics) and easy (learning instruction meaning) parts are solved separately.

hidden.name: physical affordances
paras: Physical affordances are invisible properties of what a robot can do: how soft the gripper closes, where objects slip, the stiffness of contacts, the speed the arm can move, how the camera sees the gripper relative to targets. The model needs to learn these from raw pixels, but the abstract never names this quantity explicitly.

The paper measures affordances implicitly through the model's ability to predict actions given image pairs. If the model can predict 'what action bridges frame A to frame B' correctly, it has learned the physics. The attention maps in Figure 5 show this: the pretrained model's focus automatically lands on the gripper and target object, proving it discovered the relevant affordances without human annotation.

heat.caption: Darker means more relevant to predicting robot action. The model learns which image features matter.

reads.html: The paper discovers that robots can learn to grasp and move by watching themselves play, without being told what task to do. This self-taught motor knowledge can then be re-used for any task.

The inverse dynamics objective (predicting action from observation pairs) acts as a self-supervised signal that forces the encoder to extract dynamics-aware representations—encodings that capture 'how the world changes' rather than 'what the world looks like.'

paras: The mechanism relies on a constraint: to predict an action from two consecutive images, the model must learn which pixels matter. A gripper pixel matters because it moves when the action is 'close'. A target object matters because it tells you if the action succeeded. Background pixels don't predict anything because changing the background doesn't change the action the robot should take—the loss stays zero whether the background is ignored or learned, so gradient-based training (which nudges weights toward lower loss) steers the model to ignore background and focus on the gripper. This is forced by the inverse dynamics objective itself.

Stage 1 solves a pure physics problem: 'what action would cause this before-image to become this after-image?' The model has no task label, no language instruction, no reward signal. It only has pixel-change prediction. This constraint eliminates task-specific noise and forces genuine physical understanding.

Stage 2 is cheap because the encoder already knows the physics. The decoder just needs to map 'push pumpkin left' to 'apply leftward force on the pumpkin now in view'—a simple translation from language to the motor primitives the encoder already speaks. Minimal expert video suffices because the hard part (learning what happens when you move) is solved.

stages.s: Predict action that would bridge the frames
Loss penalizes wrong predictions; encoder refines
Learned motor priors: physics is captured

math.words: loss equals the squared error between the predicted action and the true action that caused the frame change
math.equation: L_id = mean( (a_predicted - a_true)^2 ) where a_predicted = decoder( encoder(frame_t, frame_t+1) )
symbols: inverse dynamics loss (how wrong the prediction is)
the action the model guesses would cause the frame change
the action that actually happened (recorded in the robot trajectory)
the visual system that learns affordances from image pairs
the action head that turns affordances into motor commands

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Frames show gripper closed in frame_t, open in frame_t+1. True action is 'open gripper 30%'.
Model predicts 'open gripper 35%' (error = 5% units of motion).
After many such examples, encoder learns 'open gripper' is linked to frame pixels showing gripper and target object.
Stage 2 adds language: 'pick up the block' now routes through the encoder that already knows grasping.

math.note: The encoder learns affordances because predicting actions requires understanding which pixels control the robot's motion.

charts.title: No pretraining (standard behavior cloning)
charts.note: Model saturates early; limited by how much a decoder alone can learn from small expert set.

charts.title: With task-agnostic pretraining
charts.note: Pretraining does not accelerate convergence; it expands the ceiling. The encoder's learned affordances let the decoder reach higher performance.

items.html: If pretraining data comes from a robot with different arm kinematics, gripper design, or workspace than the target task, affordances won't transfer. The gripper physics the model learned do not apply.
If Stage 2 expert data uses vague instructions ('move things') the decoder cannot map language consistently to motor primitives. The affordances are learned, but the language-to-action bridge fails.

If the camera moves, lighting changes, or background shifts between pretraining and deployment, the affordance representations may not generalize. However, the paper shows pretraining keeps working when baselines fail under camera perturbation—a key strength.

Pretraining on diverse, cheap robot play (off-task trajectories from multiple robots) gives the encoder broad physical priors. Stage 2 on clean, well-annotated expert video teaches the language mapping without overfitting to a narrow task.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a two-stage learner on a toy robotic arm (or simulation): (1) Stage 1 trains inverse dynamics on 10 hours of autonomous robot play (no task labels, just 'move randomly and record'). (2) Stage 2 fine-tunes on 10 expert trajectories of 'push red cube left'. (3) Measure success rate on held-out test tasks—pushing the cube in new directions, from new start poses. Compare against a single-stage baseline (same architecture, trained end-to-end on the same 10 expert trajectories). The demo succeeds if pretraining matches or exceeds the baseline despite using the same amount of labeled data, proving that affordances learned from unlabeled play are transferable.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (number of test pushes that land in the target zone) / (total test attempts)
demo.closing: The metric must show: pretrained model reaches higher success on held-out tasks than same-architecture model trained only on expert data, using identical labeled data volume.
